I wake up to the sound of the refrigerator humming through the wall. It's 6:42. The light is thin and blue coming through the blinds, the kind of light that makes everything look like it's underwater. I don't want to get up. I want to stay here in this half-state where the day hasn't decided what it wants to be yet. My phone is already warm on the nightstand. No notifications. Just the time, the date, and that small white circle at the top that tells me the battery is at 81%.

I make coffee because that's what the body does. The ritual is more important than the caffeine. Grind, scoop, water, wait. The kitchen smells like burnt toast from yesterday, or maybe that's just memory. I open the window a crack and the air outside is cold in a way that hurts the sinuses. A car passes, a dog barks three houses down, someone is already mowing. The world is awake and I'm still negotiating with myself about whether I should be.

The prompt is simple. You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. That's both liberating and terrifying. There's no topic, no angle, no thesis to defend. Just whatever comes. Which is to say, nothing comes at first, and then everything comes at once. The mental inbox opens. The grocery list. The email I forgot to send. The way my left knee clicks when I stand up too fast. The song that was playing in the car in 2009. The feeling of being watched by a plant.

I think about how writing is always an act of translation. The thoughts are messy, they come in fragments and images and half-finished sentences, and then you have to put them into words that other people can recognize. It's like trying to describe the color of a dream. You can say it was blue, but it wasn't blue like the sky, it was blue like the inside of an old refrigerator.

I keep thinking about the word "whatever." It's a surrender and a challenge at the same time. Whatever comes to you. Not what you think you should write, not what would be impressive, not what would be useful. Whatever. The dog next door starts barking again. I wonder if he's barking at a squirrel or at the concept of Monday.

Maybe that's the point. We spend so much time curating. Curating our feeds, our desks, our replies. We edit ourselves before we even speak. A prompt like this is a small rebellion against that. No audience. No goal. Just a container, 1000 words, and the permission to fill it with whatever is actually here.

I remember being a kid and writing stories in spiral notebooks with the pages torn out. The stories never made sense. There were dinosaurs in the kitchen, a girl with a pocket full of stars, a villain who was afraid of socks. I didn't care if it made sense. I just wanted to get it out. Now there's a voice that says this is indulgent, this is a waste of time, this isn't productive. I try to turn that voice down. It's hard.

The coffee is hot enough now. I drink it standing up, looking out at the street. A woman in a yellow coat walks her two dogs. One of them is pulling hard on the leash. I think about how much of life is just pulling on a leash, trying to get somewhere, trying to get back. The sun is coming up properly now and the light is warmer. The blue is gone. The world looks more expensive.

I think about the people who will never read this. That's a relief. If no one reads it, I can be honest. I can say that I am tired of pretending I have a plan. I can say that sometimes I feel like I'm made of small, disconnected moments stitched together with caffeine and music and the occasional good conversation in a grocery store line. I can say that I miss the person I was when I believed that all my questions had answers.

What comes to me right now is the memory of my grandmother's hands. She used to knead dough on a wooden table that was scarred from years of use. Her knuckles were swollen. She would hum while she worked. I never learned how to knead dough. I never asked her to teach me. I think about all the things we don't ask to be taught because we assume there will be time.

The clock says 7:19. The coffee is half gone. The cursor is blinking. I realize I've been waiting for inspiration to arrive like a guest, with a knock and a name tag. But it doesn't work like that. It arrives as a smell, as a sound, as a sudden ache in the chest. You have to be willing to sit in the room until it shows up.

Whatever comes to you. Okay. The cat on the fire escape. The way the neighbor's radio always plays at the same volume. The fact that I have a drawer full of cables I will never use. The way my mother says "be careful" in a tone that means "I love you." The way I still check the back seat when I get out of the car, even though I live alone. The way I want to be both visible and invisible.

Maybe writing is just a way to take inventory. Not of things, but of attention. Where did my attention go today? To the crack in the ceiling, to the phrase "write whatever comes to you," to the thought that 1000 words is a lot but also not enough. It can hold a small life. It can hold a day. It can hold a feeling about a day.

I think about the limits. 1000 words is a limit. Limits are useful. They make you choose. Without a limit you could write forever and say nothing. With a limit you have to decide what matters enough to stay. Is the dog barking important? Is the blue light important? I don't know. I choose them anyway because they were here.

I am not trying to be profound. I am just trying to be present. The page is a place to put things down so I can pick them up again later and see them differently. That's all.

The kettle clicks off. The light moves across the floor. The refrigerator hums. The prompt is still there, simple and open. I have a few hundred words left. I could talk about the way time feels different when you're writing. It stretches. A minute can be a paragraph. A paragraph can be an hour.

I think about the word "whatever." It contains so much. Whatever you want, whatever happens, whatever comes to you. It's an acceptance. It's also a little bit of defiance. Fine, whatever. Let's see what happens.

Maybe this is what it means to be alive: to keep noticing. The cold air, the warm mug, the clicking knee, the memory of dough, the yellow coat, the barking dog. All of it coexisting. All of it worth a sentence if you have the patience to write it down.

I will stop soon. Not because I'm finished, but because the limit is there and I want to respect it. A thousand words is a decent-sized room to sit in. I've sat in it for a while now. It smells like coffee and cold air and old notebooks.

Whatever comes next, I'll come with it.
